passage:
Dear Hafsa Appi,
Board results came out on Wednesday. It's Sunday and I still haven't looked. The link is sitting in my messages. Ammi thinks I'm being cool about it. I'm not.
Every time I pick up the phone my stomach drops, so I put it down and go play cricket in the lane. For about an hour I forget. Then at night I lie there doing sums: if maths went badly, if I don't get science stream, if everyone asks.
The worst part is that Karim sir said the re-evaluation forms close on Tuesday, and I don't even know if I need one.
Can you call me tomorrow evening? If you're on the phone, I think I can open it.
Your little brother,
Noor

qa.q: When did the board results come out?
qa.a: Board results came out on Wednesday.

qa.q: What is Noor feeling each time he picks up the phone?
qa.a: His stomach drops with dread about a bad score; putting the phone down gives an hour of relief, but at night the worry comes back bigger.

qa.q: Is Noor's plan to open the result with Hafsa on the phone a good one?
qa.a: Yes; a calm person on the line makes it easier to look, and knowing by Monday leaves time to decide about the re-evaluation form before Tuesday.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Hafsa would likely feel tender and a little worried 🤍, glad Noor asked for help and eager to call so he isn't facing it alone.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy avoiding his exam results to put off the sting, while not knowing makes him more anxious and less prepared.

passage:
Okay Pradeep, since you asked. Me, Siddharth, the guy who hid a sealed envelope for nine days. The school sent our report cards home sealed, and I just knew physics had gone badly. So I put the envelope under my cricket kit in the cupboard and didn't touch it.
Every day it sat there I felt worse. I couldn't eat properly, I kept checking whether Mummy had cleaned the cupboard. I'd tell myself, tomorrow, I'll open it tomorrow.
Then the class group chat said physics remedial classes had started, and the signed report card was due. Mummy saw that before I did. When we finally opened it, physics was bad, yes, but not the disaster I'd been imagining. And I had already missed three remedial classes. That's the part that really hurt.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth hide the report card envelope?
qa.a: Siddharth put the envelope under the cricket kit in the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth keep promising to open it tomorrow?
qa.a: Not looking put off the sting of a bad physics mark, so each delay felt like a small relief, even though the worry grew every day.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: By hiding the result Siddharth missed three remedial classes; opening it on day one, maybe with Mummy, would make the bad news smaller and leave time to act.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy to learn about the report card from the class group chat?
qa.a: Mummy may feel hurt and worried at finding out from other parents, and sorry that Siddharth carried the fear alone for nine days.

grounding: It shows a teenager postponing the sting of a report card, which only leaves the teenager more anxious and less prepared.

passage:
I'm Sangeeta, Tushar's didi, and I watched this whole thing from the next room. The unit test marks went up on the school portal on Monday. His classmate Gopika messaged him, "Marks are up!!" Tushar turned his phone face down.
All week he said he'd check later. He was jumpy at dinner, snapped at Amma about nothing, and stayed up late watching videos. I can't say for sure what was going on inside him, but he looked like someone carrying something heavy.
On Friday I sat on his bed and said, "Want to look together? Whatever it is, it's just one test." He was quiet for a long time, then handed me the phone. Chemistry was low. He exhaled, like it was almost a relief to finally know.

qa.q: Who told Tushar the marks were up?
qa.a: His classmate Gopika messaged him, "Marks are up!!"

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling during the week he didn't check?
qa.a: He was probably anxious about a bad mark and dreading the sting; being jumpy, snapping at Amma and staying up late suggest the not-knowing weighed on him more than the mark itself.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta help Tushar face the result?
qa.a: Sangeeta offered to look together and made it smaller by saying it was just one test, so Tushar could hand over the phone without feeling judged.

qa.q: How is Amma affected by Tushar's week of avoiding the marks?
qa.a: She gets snapped at for nothing, taking the edge of a worry she doesn't even know about.

grounding: It shows, through an older sister's eyes, a teenage boy avoiding his test marks to delay the sting while the not-knowing makes him more anxious.

passage:
Tuesday: The class group buzzed at four: "Half-yearly results on the school app!" Yash, fourteen, put his phone in the drawer and went to play football till dark. At dinner his mother, Rashmi, asked, "Results?" "Not out yet," he said, and his stomach turned.
Friday: At maths tuition, Sir began going over the half-yearly paper. Everyone else had checked their marks and brought questions. Yash hadn't looked. He sat with his notebook closed, heart thumping, not following a word.
Sunday: Rashmi found him awake at one in the morning. He finally opened the app with her beside him. Maths was bad: 41. Science was fine. "Okay," Rashmi said. "Now we know what to fix." Yash let out a long breath. The number was smaller than the fear had been.

qa.q: Where did Yash put his phone when the results came out?
qa.a: He put his phone in the drawer.

qa.q: Why might not checking the app have felt better to Yash on Tuesday?
qa.a: Avoiding the marks postponed the sting of a bad result, so for a few hours he could pretend nothing had changed.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Opening the app on Sunday with his mother beside him; once he knew maths was the problem he could start fixing it, and the fear shrank 🙂

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt finding Yash awake at one?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and tender, realising the results had been weighing on him for days.

grounding: A teenage boy avoids checking his results to put off the sting, and the not-knowing leaves him more anxious and lost in class.

passage: Sahil, you've been hiding that report card envelope under your pillow since Friday. Your Mola Dolma knows everything. Let me tell you about my brother Pasang. In Darjeeling, when we were young, results were pinned on the school gate. Pasang was fifteen. The day they went up, he took the long road home, round the tea garden, so he wouldn't pass the gate. For two weeks he wouldn't let anyone say the word "results". He barely slept, and he snapped at our mother. Then the teacher came to our house. Pasang had failed one subject, and the re-test was in four days. Four days, when he could have had two weeks. He passed, just. But he always said the waiting was worse than the marks. So. Shall we open it together, over tea?

qa.q: Why did Pasang take the long road home round the tea garden?
qa.a: So he wouldn't pass the gate where the results were pinned.

qa.q: Why do you think Pasang wouldn't let anyone say the word "results"?
qa.a: Hearing it brought the dread closer, so blocking it out gave him a little relief, even though he barely slept.

qa.q: What choice does Dolma offer Sahil, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To open the envelope together over tea, so Sahil faces the news early and with company, leaving time to act instead of losing days to fear.

qa.q: What might those two weeks have been like for Pasang's mother?
qa.a: She had to live with his snapping and sleepless nights without knowing why, which was likely worrying and hurtful.

grounding: An elder recalls a brother avoiding his results, which left him anxious and with less time to prepare for a re-test.
